<reason>Side B built the stronger case on information asymmetry and informed consent, anchoring the debate in the material difference between hidden hazards and disclosed conditions. While Side A raised sharp implementation concerns (perverse incentives, boilerplate, liability), Side B adequately defended against them by proposing objective documentation standards, rolling disclosure windows, and mandatory logging requirements. Side A's alternative of tenant self-inspection during viewings was underdeveloped, failing to address how renters could discover historical complaint patterns or third-party behavior. Side B's clipped closing was an execution cost, but the overall arc favored the proposition.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 attack on Side B's "rolling window" fix, exposing the fraud liability trap that would force landlords to use permanent boilerplate, which Side B could only partially neutralize by narrowing the standard to "current risk at signing."</best_rebuttal>
